strengths: Strong empirical results on multiple datasets: 10-12% improvements on PSM, MSL, SMD; 4.71% on WADI with online applicability
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 benchmark datasets, 15 baseline comparisons, thorough ablation studies (Tables 4-5), robustness assessment with multiple random seeds
Novel combination of techniques: causal MLP-Mixer enforcement, cluster-aware multi-embedding, and sequential anomaly scoring for the time series anomaly detection task
Practical online approach: method operates in real-time without requiring full test set access, addressing limitations of offline methods like SensitiveHUE

Solid technical foundation: spectral clustering on correlation profiles is well-motivated, causal masking approach is mathematically sound, ablation studies clearly demonstrate component contributions
weaknesses: Inconsistent performance on major benchmarks: -3.07% degradation on SWaT (0.883 vs 0.911 SensitiveHUE Offline) and 0% improvement on SMAP undermine claims of consistent superiority

Critical technical details lack justification: the 1/j normalization factor in causal masking (Eq. 11) is unexplained and arbitrary; embedding dimension allocation for small clusters not discussed; reset condition in Eq. 15 uses strict AND requiring all past δ steps negative evidence

Incomplete spurious correlation mitigation: Appendix G shows clustering only reduces spurious correlations by ~28-30%, not eliminating them. Authors acknowledge common embedding mixer and head layer still mix all channels, contradicting the clustering motivation

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity: extensive tuning required (M∈[1,10], α∈[0,1], d_f∈{1,3,5}); α and threshold h demand dataset-specific optimization via Optuna; Appendix H admits sensitivity to α and small datasets limits generalizability

Limited theoretical novelty and unclear benefits: causal masking is standard in transformers yet distinction/advantages over transformer causality not clearly articulated; non-causal temporal mixer (Case 8) performs nearly identically to full model, questioning causality's actual utility

Lack of statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests on improvements; no sensitivity analysis for critical parameters α, h, δ; baseline results largely from prior papers rather than independent runs
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; complex, dataset-specific preprocessing (Appendix C) is error-prone; baseline comparisons potentially inconsistent across implementations

Missing theoretical justification and analysis: no explanation for why causality helps anomaly detection; backward search using argmax (Eq. 16-17) is brittle with multiple time steps potentially satisfying conditions; impact on detection latency and false negatives within anomaly sequences not analyzed

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 6 benchmark datasets against 15 baselines with detailed ablation studies (Tables 4-5)
Solid empirical improvements on several datasets (PSM +10.32%, MSL +12.34%, SMD +11.96%, WADI +4.71%)
Honest discussion of limitations in Appendix H, including sensitivity to hyperparameter α and incomplete spurious correlation mitigation
Good reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters (Table 6), implementation details, and computational costs (Table 7)
Multiple ablation studies examining different architectural components and clustering variants
weaknesses: Limited novelty: causal masking via upper-triangular weight masks is a straightforward application of existing techniques (like attention masking in transformers), not a conceptual advance; spectral clustering on correlation profiles is standard; sequential scoring is ad-hoc without theoretical justification
Inconsistent results across datasets: method regresses on SWaT (-3.07% vs SensitiveHUE Offline) and shows zero improvement on SMAP (0.00%), suggesting lack of generality
Unfair baseline comparison: compares against SensitiveHUE (Online), which deliberately uses a degraded version with removed normalization; this is cherry-picking rather than principled comparison

Fundamental design flaw acknowledged in Appendix G: clustering-based multi-embedding does not mitigate spurious correlations because the common embedding mixer and head layer re-mix all embeddings together, defeating the clustering purpose

Incomplete ablation of causal contribution: Table 4 shows non-causal (Case-8, F1=0.661 on PSM) and causal (Case-10, F1=0.716) mixers, but improvement is small and Case-6 (no mixer, F1=0.657) performs similarly to Case-8, leaving causality's individual contribution unclear

Excessive hyperparameter tuning complexity: requires optimizing M, α, h, δ, learning rate, df, d separately per dataset (Table 6 shows different ranges) with high sensitivity to α acknowledged in Appendix H; impractical for deployment on new datasets
High variance on multi-entity datasets (Table 7: SMAP std=0.025 on mean 0.564, MSL std=0.024 on mean 0.622) raises stability concerns
No computational cost comparison to baselines: Table 7 reports GFLOPs but no comparison whether 17.129 for WADI is better/worse than alternatives; clustering overhead not quantified
Dataset-specific preprocessing (Appendix C) undermines generalization claims and makes reproducibility harder; different preprocessing for different datasets suggests method lacks robustness

Ad-hoc anomaly detection method: p-value based scoring (Eq. 14) and evidence accumulation with resets (Eq. 15) lack theoretical grounding; backward search procedure (Eqs. 16-17) is heuristic without justification; multiple hyperparameters require tuning

strengths: Addresses genuine limitations of existing methods: MLP-Mixers lacking causality and single embeddings failing to capture diverse inter-channel correlations
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 benchmark datasets, 15 baselines, substantial improvements on 4/6 datasets (PSM +10.32%, MSL +12.34%, SMD +11.96%, WADI +4.71%)
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 3-5) clearly demonstrating contribution of each component; additional analysis of spurious correlation reduction (27.98% on PSM)
True online applicability distinguishes method from offline competitors like SensitiveHUE, with demonstrated robustness across multiple seeds

Well-structured technical presentation with correct mathematical formulations (causal masking, spectral clustering algorithm, sequential scoring) and detailed reproducibility information in appendices
Honest discussion of limitations (Appendix H) including sensitivity to α, dataset size effects, and incomplete spurious correlation mitigation
weaknesses: Mixed empirical results weaken central claims: SWaT shows -3.07% regression vs. SensitiveHUE (Offline), SMAP achieves 0.00% improvement; claims of 'superior F1 scores' do not hold uniformly across datasets

Insufficient justification for causality in anomaly detection: paper motivates causality for forecasting but fails to explain why it matters for reconstruction-based anomaly detection; modest ablation gains (Table 4: +1.4% SWAT, +5.1% PSM) don't convincingly demonstrate necessity

Limited fundamental novelty: causal masking is straightforward application of existing technique, spectral clustering is standard, sequential scoring is intuitive but not novel; main contribution is combination rather than innovation

Cluster robustness concerns: correlation-based clustering computed only from training data without analysis of sensitivity to distribution shift; optimal cluster numbers vary per dataset (M=4-6, Table 5) with limited sensitivity analysis

Sequential anomaly detection method is ad-hoc: p-value approach (Eq. 14) assumes validation loss is reliable test proxy, backward search (Eqs. 16-17) is heuristic without theoretical justification, introduces multiple hyperparameters (α, h, δ) with limited δ exploration

Incomplete ablation coverage: Table 4 shows full ablation only for SWAT and PSM; isolated contributions of clustering and causality not evaluated across all datasets, limiting generalizability of findings

Hyperparameter tuning per-dataset via Optuna may provide unfair advantage over baselines using fixed hyperparameters; statistical significance testing limited to standard deviations without confidence intervals

Computational cost under-explored: only GFLOPs reported (Table 7) without runtime/memory comparisons; WADI's high cost (17.129 GFLOPs) not compared to baselines, overhead of multiple embedding layers not quantified

strengths: Well-motivated identification of temporal causality limitation in MLP-Mixer models, with sound technical solution verified via gradient analysis (Figure 3)
Consistent and substantial empirical improvements across six diverse datasets (8.71% on WADI, 8.65% on PSM, up to 41.2% on multi-entity MSL), with comprehensive comparison against 23 baselines

Comprehensive and systematic experimental evaluation including multiple evaluation protocols, multiple metrics (Best-F1, PR-AUC, VUS-PR, VUS-ROC), ablation studies validating each component, robustness analysis over 5 random seeds, and computational cost analysis
Addresses practical online anomaly detection scenario where prior work (SensitiveHUE) requires offline access to full test set statistics, enabling real-time deployment
Thorough presentation with excellent reproducibility: code available, detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, implementation details provided, honest limitation discussion in Appendix M

Strong technical execution of cluster-aware multi-embedding approach with statistical grounding (Appendix A) and representation separability analysis showing 39% improvement in nearest-neighbor separation on SWAT
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: paper combines three existing techniques (causal masking as straightforward extension of attention masking, standard spectral clustering, existing sequential scoring) without introducing fundamental new concepts

Critical assumption of clean training data not validated experimentally—paper acknowledges contamination may degrade performance but provides no robustness tests or evaluation on datasets with training set anomalies

Statistical validity concerns: empirical p-value approximation to U(0,1) assumes high-quality model reconstruction, but this depends on dataset characteristics; for entity-wise models with limited validation data, α searches full [0,1) space risking overfitting

Incremental improvements on some datasets: SWAT baseline (SensitiveHUE Offline 0.911) outperforms proposed method (0.883); PSM improvements modest (8.65%); VUS-ROC results inconsistent across datasets

Temporal causality scope narrower than suggested: method enforces temporal order only, not inter-channel causality or causal discovery; boundary refinement (Eq. 16-17) assumes clear onset/offset unsuitable for gradual anomalies

Dense paper with many interacting components (clustering, causal mixer, embedding mixer, sequential scoring) making critical contributions unclear; design choices (1/j normalization, proportional embedding dimensions) lack explicit justification

Static clustering based on training correlations without adaptation to test distribution shifts; NaN correlation handling through simple grouping may be suboptimal; no analysis of failure cases or anomaly type performance

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets and 23 baselines with consistent improvements and thorough ablation studies (Table 5)
Rigorous validation of causality claims via gradient-based analysis (Figure 3) demonstrating effective suppression of future information leakage
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameter ranges, algorithms, and data processing procedures in appendices
Practical online anomaly detection without requiring access to future test data, addressing a limitation of SensitiveHUE(Offline)
Multiple evaluation metrics (Best-F1, PR AUC, VUS PR, VUS ROC, ADD-FAP) demonstrating robustness across different evaluation frameworks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: causal masking is a straightforward application of transformer attention masking to MLPs, spectral clustering is standard, and sequential scoring lacks conceptual innovation (Table 7 shows only marginal gains over K-means baseline)

Weak motivation for component interactions: paper does not explain why causal mixing, cluster-aware embedding, and sequential scoring work synergistically, providing only additive ablation results without mechanistic insight

Overstated 'causality' framing: method enforces only temporal ordering, not causal relationships; connection to causal inference is unclear and the paper oversells this as core contribution despite limitations section clarifying the distinction

Modest empirical improvements with inconsistent results: SWAT underperforms SensitiveHUE(Offline) by 3% (0.883 vs 0.911), PSM shows only 2.3% gain (0.716 vs 0.700), and main results lack confidence intervals or statistical significance testing

Flawed statistical foundation: sequential anomaly scoring assumes p-value uniformity (Eq. 14) but Figure 4 reveals temporal correlations in reconstruction loss violating i.i.d. assumptions; implications for method validity are unaddressed

High complexity and hyperparameter sensitivity: method requires tuning M, α, h, δ, d, df across datasets; clustering depends on training correlations with limited robustness analysis to distribution shifts (Appendix J.5 shows only 0.878-0.883 range)

Incomplete ablations: no analysis of how components contribute to different anomaly types or failure modes; Figure 12 shows non-monotonic sensitivity to embedding dimension d, suggesting optimization landscape complexity not addressed

Missing code and vague online claim: 'code available at' link is placeholder; 'online' framing is partially misleading as method requires offline validation set pre-computation, with only sequential scoring being genuinely online

strengths: Well-motivated technical approach addressing specific limitations of existing MLP-Mixer models and transformer-based anomaly detection methods

Technically sound methodology with rigorous validation: causal masking proven via gradient analysis (Figure 3), spectral clustering grounded in established theory, statistical anomaly detection with probability analysis (Appendix A)

Comprehensive experimental validation across 6 benchmark datasets, 23 baselines, multiple evaluation protocols (3 for multi-entity datasets), and multiple metrics (Best-F1, PR-AUC, VUS-PR, VUS-ROC, ADD-FAP)
Consistent and meaningful empirical improvements: +8.71% on WADI, +8.65% on PSM, up to +41.2% on MSL, with consistent gains across all multi-entity datasets under all protocols

Excellent reproducibility documentation including detailed hyperparameter ranges (Table 9), hardware specifications, library versions, preprocessing details (Appendix D), and robustness analysis with multiple seeds (Table 12)
True online applicability without requiring access to entire test set, with low inference latency (milliseconds per batch) and reduced computational cost compared to SensitiveHUE(Online)

Thorough ablation studies systematically isolating component contributions: 10 model configurations (Table 5), clustering variants (Table 7), sensitivity analyses (Figures 10-12), gradient-based causality verification (Figure 3)

Honest and comprehensive limitations discussion acknowledging focus on temporal (not Granger) causality, requirement for clean training data, unsuitability for univariate data, and clustering dependence on training correlation patterns
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: causal masking is essentially attention masking applied to MLPs, spectral clustering is standard technique, multi-embedding is straightforward concatenation; primary novelty lies in combination rather than methodological innovation

Clustering methodology concerns: requires offline computation from training data without capability to adapt to test-time distributional shifts; while robustness to moderate shifts shown (Appendix J.5), substantial shifts may require re-clustering and no systematic evaluation of performance degradation

Causality framing and justification inadequately supported: temporal causality is proven via gradient analysis (Figure 3) but the mechanism by which it improves anomaly detection deserves more rigorous justification; ablation shows modest causal benefit on PSM (0.657 vs 0.652)

Critical assumption of clean training data not empirically validated despite being identified as important limitation; no evaluation of robustness to training contamination, which is common in real-world scenarios with unlabeled anomalies in training sets

Hyperparameter tuning complexity with multiple parameters requiring dataset-specific optimization (M, α, h, d, δ, df, L); Optuna-based tuning and principled but ad-hoc bounds for α (Appendix G.1) suggest limited generalization to new domains

Sequential anomaly scoring contains ad-hoc design choices: reset condition using δ consecutive negative evidences lacks rigorous justification; 1/j scaling in causal mask motivated by optimization stability (Appendix J.4) rather than theory; boundary refinement (Eqs. 16-17) is heuristic

Performance improvements vary considerably across datasets: substantial gains on WADI/PSM/MSL but marginal improvements on others (PSM NN-sep: +0.06%), and competitive rather than dominant PR-AUC performance on PSM dataset

Incomplete baseline analysis: SensitiveHUE(Online) and some other baselines reimplemented by authors introducing potential implementation gaps; missing discussion of failure cases and dataset characteristics favoring CCM-TAD; limited analysis of when method underperforms
